In ‘The Odyssey’, when Odysseus first approaches his manor house he weeps at the sight of his old dog Argos, “abandoned” on a dung heap outside the gates. The dog struggles to greet his master, “but death and darkness in that instant closed / the eyes of Argos, who had seen his master / Odysseus, after twenty year”
Thy will be done – After the Lord’s prayer: “Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven”

children: Typical snippets of obituary-column prose, “The Little Flower” is a popular name for St. Teresa of Lisieux (St. Teresa-of-the-Child-Jesus, 1873-97), whose cultus grew with such rapidity and intensity after her death that ‘Butler’s’ “Lives of the Saints” calls it “the most impressive and significant religious phenomenon of contemporary times”. St Teresa (beatified in 1923, canonized in 1925) promised: “After my death I will let fall a shower of roses”; hence her nickname, “The Little Flower.”

Another “little flower,” a poem by Tennyson titled “Flower in the Crannied Wall” (1869), appears at the top of the right-hand column of the ‘Evening Telegraph’ of 16 June 1904 under the heading “Gleaned from All Sources”: “Flower in the crannied wall, / I pluck you out of the crannies, / I hold you here, root and all, in my hand, / Little Flower-but if I could understand / What you are, root and all, and all in all, / I should know what God and man is.”
Month’s mind: a commemorative requiem mass said on the thirteenth day after death.

The melodramatic tangle is compounded by Creegan’s pride; by a pettifogging [placing undue emphasis on petty details; petty or trivial] lawyer with a mortgage to foreclose unless Mrs. Creegan marries him; by Creegan’s faithful servant, whose mistaken zeal leads him to attempt to murder Eily; by the lawyer, who has Creegan arrested for the murder that has not been committed; etc. All is resolved by relevation and confession: Creegan is reunited with Eily, Anne marries Kyrle, the mortgage blows away, and the lawyer is ducked in the horsepond.

From medicine.net

A remarkable phenomenon in which a placebo – a fake treatment, an inactive substance like sugar, distilled water, or saline solution – can sometimes improve a patient’s condition simply because the person has the expectation that it will be helpful.

The placebo effect, although widely documented, is poorly understood and remains something of a mystery. Research has also shown that the effect can still be observed even when the patient is told that what they are receving is a placebo; and that a “placebo injection” is often more effective than a placeb pill.

23424799.twitter_share_message: “I think Bloom is musing about Catholicism and Judaism.  In Judaism, a deceased body is always gu…” —@Genius

children: I think Bloom is musing about Catholicism and Judaism.  In Judaism, a deceased body is always guarded, never left alone.  Washing the body is a ritual, considered a mitzvah, and done in conjunction with prayers and blessings.  To just leave this job to the women of the town or family, to leave the corpse unattended, and to not follow the rituals would be considered “unclean”, or not in accordance with Kosher laws in their broader application.  A devout Jew may not know specifically who might touch him dead, but is assured that he will be treated with respect and reverence.

Cutting and disposing of fingernails is also ritualistic in Judaism, though I don’t know what is to be done with the nail and hair clippings of the deceased.  I don’t imagine keeping them in an envelope is approved.
Interesting that his musings are about shampoo, washing, and cleanliness – and he is transported from being “in his head” back to the physical world by the reality of the soap in his pocket.
